## Course description

Number theory is the study of the positive integers and the remarkable structures hidden inside them. Although its questions are often easy to state, many have resisted centuries of effort. This course introduces divisibility, congruences, prime numbers, Diophantine equations, quadratic residues, and selected classical applications. Throughout the course, we will emphasize proof writing, experimentation, mathematical communication, and the transition from examples to general theorems.

## Learning objectives

By the end of the course, students should be able to:

1. use the Euclidean algorithm, Bézout's identity, and unique factorization fluently;
2. solve linear congruences and systems of congruences;
3. apply Fermat's little theorem, Euler's theorem, and related results;
4. analyze classical Diophantine equations and quadratic residues;
5. write clear proofs using direct, contrapositive, contradiction, and induction arguments;
6. use computation to explore examples while distinguishing evidence from proof.

## Prerequisites

[State the formal prerequisites.] Students should be comfortable with algebraic manipulation, functions, sets, and basic proof techniques. Prior exposure to proof-based mathematics is helpful.

## Recommended textbook

W. J. LeVeque, *Fundamentals of Number Theory*.

The book covers the standard topics clearly and is remarkably inexpensive. It is recommended but not required. Lecture notes, examples, and assignments will be posted on this website.

## Homework

Homework will be assigned every one or two weeks. Late homework will not normally be accepted, although early submission or an extension may be arranged in advance when circumstances require it. The lowest homework score will be dropped at the end of the term.

Collaboration is encouraged, but every student must understand and write the final solutions independently. You should be able to explain every submitted argument in detail. Copying from another student, a textbook solution source, or an unauthorized website is not permitted.

## Exams

There are two in-class midterm examinations and a cumulative final examination. Exams are closed book and closed notes unless announced otherwise. No make-up examinations will be given except when required by university policy or arranged for a documented emergency.
